claims.text: Documentation sets commonly sort pages into roughly four kinds — a beginner walkthrough, a task recipe, a lookup listing and a why-page — and the labels differ per site (Task or How-to; Concept or Explanation).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io/docs contribute/style/page-content-types — the four page content types Concept, Task, Tutorial, Reference

claims.text: A tutorial covers a goal larger than a single task and has its own sequence of steps; a task or how-to page shows how to do one named thing, with minimal explanation.
A reference page lists what exists — the options, their defaults, the errors; a concept or explanation page gives the reasons behind the design and typically contains no sequence of steps.
When you want one option, default or error message, jumping to that entry is usually faster than reading the reference page from the top.
Official documentation sites usually publish one set of pages per release and offer a version selector near the top of the page to switch between them.
claims.source_hint: postgresql.org/docs/17/ — the 'Supported Versions' bar at the top of the page

claims.text: The version a documentation site shows by default is not always the release the reader is running.
claims.source_hint: postgresql.org/docs — 'Current' in the version bar points at the newest release, not at the one pinned in content/versions.yaml

claims.text: When a documentation page and observed behaviour disagree, the first three things to check are the version the page describes, the version being run, and an assumption the reader made about their own setup.
At tag stage-0, running scripts/http/cache-headers.sh prints a response whose headers include 'Cache-Control: max-age=60'.
At tag stage-0, docs/craft/doc-reading-checklist.md opens with four checkboxes covering the kind of information wanted, the kind of page, the page's version and the reader's version.
The same file names the recurring words of technical English: deprecated, default, required, optional, idempotent, throws, unless, at least once, must, should, may.
In a standards document the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY carry their defined requirement levels when, and only when, they appear in all capitals; the same words in lower case are ordinary English.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 section 2.2 Requirements Notation ('when, and only when, they appear in all capitals')

claims.text: MUST is an absolute requirement; SHOULD is recommended and may be departed from only for a valid reason whose full implications have been weighed; MAY is truly optional.
claims.source_hint: BCP 14 (RFC 2119) sections 1-5, imported by RFC 9110 section 2.2

claims.text: Technical documentation reuses a narrow set of words with fixed meanings, so the same words recur across products and pages.
'deprecated' means still working but no longer recommended, and often on its way out — not simply 'old'.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io/docs reference deprecation policy; learn.microsoft.com/dotnet — [Obsolete] guidance

claims.text: A blog post often omits the release it was written against and folds the author's own setup into its steps, whereas an official page usually states its version at the top.
Machine translation tends to collapse MUST / SHOULD / MAY into a single verb and to lose the precise sense of 'deprecated'.
At tag stage-0, scripts/up.sh starts the lab — the static site, the database and the lab box the other scripts talk to — and Docker Desktop is the only prerequisite for running the scripts.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: STAGE.md 'What exists at this tag'; scripts/up.sh header comment and its closing echo block

claims.text: Searching the product's own documentation site, then searching inside that site, reaches the defining page more reliably than searching the whole web.
A standard HTTP header is defined in a specification, which is a reference page; Cache-Control is defined in RFC 9111 section 5.2.
A specification is published as a fixed document and carries no version selector; its own document number identifies it instead.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 front matter and RFC Editor document format — an RFC is immutable once published, superseded rather than revised in place

claims.text: git checkout stage-0 moves a working copy of the example repository to the state saved at the tag stage-0.
